summary.text: For every \(1\le d\le2025\), a finite least-common-multiple argument using the pairs \((2,17),(3,17),(5,23),(7,19),(11,13)\) finds a pair \((p,q)\) with different final digits, \(pq\le150\), and neither prime dividing \(d\). Thus \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), so some index \(i<pq\) has \(a+id\equiv0\pmod{pq}\); that term is divisible by two primes with different final digits and therefore cannot satisfy the required condition.

full_proof.text:
Let us call a positive integer admissible if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. We prove that there cannot be integers \(a,d\) with
\[
a\ge 2,\qquad 1\le d\le 2025,
\]
such that all of
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
are admissible.

The proof uses the following five pairs of primes:
\[
(2,17),\quad (3,17),\quad (5,23),\quad (7,19),\quad (11,13).
\]
For each pair, the two primes have different final decimal digits, and their product is at most \(150\). Explicitly,
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
(p,q)&(p\bmod 10,q\bmod 10)&pq&pq\le150\\ \hline
(2,17)&(2,7)&34&\text{yes}\\
(3,17)&(3,7)&51&\text{yes}\\
(5,23)&(5,3)&115&\text{yes}\\
(7,19)&(7,9)&133&\text{yes}\\
(11,13)&(1,3)&143&\text{yes}.
\end{array}
\]

We first establish the key fact that for every positive \(d\le 2025\), at least one of these five pairs consists of two primes neither of which divides \(d\).

Suppose, to the contrary, that no pair has this property. Then each of the five pairs contains at least one prime dividing \(d\). Thus
\[
2\mid d\ \text{or}\ 17\mid d,
\]
\[
3\mid d\ \text{or}\ 17\mid d,
\]
\[
5\mid d\ \text{or}\ 23\mid d,
\]
\[
7\mid d\ \text{or}\ 19\mid d,
\]
and
\[
11\mid d\ \text{or}\ 13\mid d.
\]
We split according to whether \(17\) divides \(d\).

First suppose \(17\mid d\). From each of the last three alternatives choose a divisor of \(d\): choose
\[
x\in\{5,23\},\qquad y\in\{7,19\},\qquad z\in\{11,13\}
\]
with \(x\mid d\), \(y\mid d\), and \(z\mid d\). The four numbers \(17,x,y,z\) are distinct primes, so their product \(17xyz\) divides \(d\). The eight possible products are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
x&y&z&17xyz\\ \hline
5&7&11&6545\\
5&7&13&7735\\
5&19&11&17765\\
5&19&13&20995\\
23&7&11&30107\\
23&7&13&35581\\
23&19&11&81719\\
23&19&13&96577.
\end{array}
\]
Every one of these is greater than \(2025\). A positive integer divisible by a positive integer \(L\) is at least \(L\). Hence \(17xyz\mid d\) is incompatible with \(0<d\le2025\). This rules out the case \(17\mid d\).

Now suppose \(17\nmid d\). Since at least one member of \((2,17)\) divides \(d\), it follows that \(2\mid d\). Similarly, the pair \((3,17)\) forces \(3\mid d\). As before, choose
\[
x\in\{5,23\},\qquad y\in\{7,19\},\qquad z\in\{11,13\}
\]
so that \(x,y,z\) all divide \(d\). The five numbers \(2,3,x,y,z\) are distinct primes, and therefore \(6xyz\mid d\). The eight possible products are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
x&y&z&6xyz\\ \hline
5&7&11&2310\\
5&7&13&2730\\
5&19&11&6270\\
5&19&13&7410\\
23&7&11&10626\\
23&7&13&12558\\
23&19&11&28842\\
23&19&13&34086.
\end{array}
\]
Again, every possible product is greater than \(2025\), contradicting \(0<d\le2025\). This also rules out the case \(17\nmid d\).

Consequently, for every \(d\) with \(1\le d\le2025\), there is a pair \((p,q)\) among the five displayed pairs such that
\[
p\nmid d,\qquad q\nmid d,
\]
while \(p,q\) are prime, have different final decimal digits, and satisfy \(pq\le150\).

We now apply this fact to a purported arithmetic progression. Assume that \(a\ge2\), \(1\le d\le2025\), and every term \(a+id\), for \(0\le i<150\), is admissible. Choose the pair \((p,q)\) just obtained, and put
\[
m=pq.
\]
Because \(p\) and \(q\) are primes and neither divides \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,p)=\gcd(d,q)=1.
\]
The primes \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct—indeed, their final digits differ—so it follows that
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Thus \(d\) has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(m=pq\). In particular, the congruence
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod m
\]
has a solution modulo \(m\). More explicitly, choose an integer \(t\) satisfying
\[
dt\equiv1\pmod m.
\]
Then one may take
\[
i\equiv -at\pmod m.
\]
Choose the unique representative \(i\) with
\[
0\le i<m.
\]
Multiplying the defining congruence by \(d\) gives
\[
id\equiv-atd\equiv-a\pmod m,
\]
so
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod m.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
pq\mid a+id.
\]

The choice of the prime pair guaranteed \(pq\le150\). Since \(0\le i<pq\), we therefore have
\[
0\le i<150.
\]
Thus \(a+id\) is one of the claimed \(150\) admissible terms. It is positive, since \(a\ge2\) and \(i,d\ge0\). But \(pq\mid a+id\) implies separately that
\[
p\mid a+id\qquad\text{and}\qquad q\mid a+id.
\]
Hence both \(p\) and \(q\) occur among the prime divisors of this term. By construction, \(p\bmod10\ne q\bmod10\), so these two prime divisors have different final decimal digits. Therefore \(a+id\) is not admissible, contrary to the assumption that every one of the first \(150\) terms is admissible.

This contradiction applies to every possible \(a\ge2\) and every \(1\le d\le2025\). Hence no increasing arithmetic progression of \(150\) such numbers with common difference at most \(2025\) exists, disproving the conjecture.
